'''''Vaccinium corymbosum''''' is a North American species of [[blueberry]] with several common names, including '''highbush blueberry''' and '''rabbiteye blueberry'''.<ref name="ncsu">{{cite web|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/vaccinium-corymbosum/|title=''Vaccinium corymbosum''|publisher=North Carolina State University, Extension Cooperative|date=2026|access-date=15 January 2026}}</ref><ref name="kemper" />

The species became commonly cultivated as a fresh fruit crop in the 20th century, with dozens of commercial cultivars. It can be used as an ornamental [[hedge]] as well a food source for humans and wildlife.

==Description==
''Vaccinium corymbosum'' is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] growing to {{convert|6|-|12|ft|order=flip|m}} tall and wide. It is often found in dense thickets. The dark glossy green [[leaves]] are elliptical and up to {{convert|2|in|cm|0|order=flip}} long. In autumn, the leaves turn to a brilliant red, orange, yellow, and/or purple.<ref name="uconn">''Vaccinium corymbosum''. accessed 3.23.2013</ref><ref name=pancakes>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242417401 Flora of North America, ''Vaccinium corymbosum'' Linnaeus, 1753. High-bush blueberry, bleuet en corymbe ]</ref>

The [[flower]]s are long bell- or urn-shaped white to very light pink, {{convert|1/3|in|mm|abbr=on|adj=on|order=flip}} long.<ref name="uconn"/><ref name=pancakes/> The fruit is a blue-black [[Berry (botany)|berry]] with a {{convert|1/4|-|1/2|in|mm|abbr=on|adj=on|order=flip}} diameter.<ref name="uconn" />

The species is [[tetraploid]] and does not [[Self-pollination|self-pollinate]].<ref name="Volume21">{{cite book|last1=Retamales|first1=Jorge B.|last2=Hancock|first2=James F.|title=Blueberries: Volume 21 of Crop production science in horticulture|date=2012|publisher=Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International (CABI)|location=Cambridge, MA|isbn=9781845938260|pages=2 & 39–42|edition=1st|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=22aW1z1klDMC}}</ref> Most [[cultivars]] have a [[chilling requirement]] greater than 800 hours. [[Cytology]] is 2n = 48.<ref name="y832">{{cite journal | last1=Redpath | first1=Lauren E. | last2=Aryal | first2=Rishi | last3=Lynch | first3=Nathan | last4=Spencer | first4=Jessica A. | last5=Hulse-Kemp | first5=Amanda M. | last6=Ballington | first6=James R. | last7=Green | first7=Jaimie | last8=Bassil | first8=Nahla | last9=Hummer | first9=Kim | last10=Ranney | first10=Thomas | last11=Ashrafi | first11=Hamid | title=Nuclear DNA contents and ploidy levels of North American Vaccinium species and interspecific hybrids | journal=Scientia Horticulturae | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=297 | year=2022 | issn=0304-4238 | doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2022.110955 | article-number=110955| bibcode=2022ScHor.29710955R | doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is native to eastern Canada and the eastern and southern United States, from [[Ontario]] east to [[Nova Scotia]] and south as far as Florida and eastern [[Texas]]. It is also naturalized in other places, including Europe, Japan, New Zealand, and the North American [[Pacific Northwest]].<ref>[https://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Vaccinium%20corymbosum.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref><ref>[https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=23573 Taxonomic account from Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS) — for ''Vaccinium corymbosum'' (highbush blueberry)]</ref><ref name="uconn" /><ref name="grin">{{GRIN|access-date=2017-12-15}}</ref> 

The plant is found in wooded or open habitats with moist [[acidic soils]].<ref name="pancakes" /><ref name="kemper">[http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/gardens-gardening/your-garden/plant-finder/plant-details/kc/m690/vaccinium-corymbosum.aspx Missouri Botanical Garden: Kemper Center for Home Gardening — ''Vaccinium corymbosum'']. accessed 3.23.2013</ref>

==Ecology==
In natural habitats, the berries are a food source for native and migrating birds, bears, and small mammals. The foliage is browsed by deer and rabbits.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=509}}</ref><ref name="kemper" />

== Cultivation ==
Many wild species of ''Vaccinium'' are thought to have been cultivated by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American]]s for thousands of years, with intentional crop burnings in northeastern areas being apparent from [[archeological]] evidence.<ref name="Volume21" /> ''V. corymbosum'', being one of the species likely used by these peoples, was later studied and domesticated in 1908 by [[Elizabeth Coleman White]] and [[Frederick Vernon Coville]].{{Citation needed|date=August 2024}} It became commonly cultivated as a fresh fruit crop in the 20th century<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Gough | first1 = Robert Edward | title = The highbush blueberry and its management | publisher = Psychology Press | year = 1994 | pages = 3 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=_wqfvwUy_oAC | access-date = 2011-04-29 | isbn = 978-1-56022-021-3}}</ref><ref name="ncsu" /> and the most common commercially grown blueberry in North America.{{Citation needed|date=August 2024}}

It is also cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] for home and [[wildlife garden]]s and [[natural landscaping]] projects.<ref name="kemper" /><ref>[http://www.hort.uconn.edu/plants/v/vaccor/vaccor1.html Hort.uconn.edu: ''Vaccinium corymbosum''; Landscape use section] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130327072752/http://www.hort.uconn.edu/plants/v/vaccor/vaccor1.html |date=2013-03-27}}. accessed 3.23.2013</ref> The soil pH must be very acidic (4.5 to 5.5).<ref name="uconn" />  It can be used as an ornamental [[hedge]].<ref name="kemper" />

The cultivars ''Duke''<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Vaccinium corymbosum'' 'Duke'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/57014/Vaccinium-corymbosum-Duke-(F)/Details | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref> and ''Spartan''<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Vaccinium corymbosum'' 'Spartan'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/80821/Vaccinium-corymbosum-Spartan-(F)/Details | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].

=== Southern highbush blueberry ===
Some plants named southern highbush blueberry are [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridized]] forms derived from crosses between ''V. corymbosum'' and ''[[Vaccinium darrowii|V. darrowii]]'', a native of the Southeastern US. These hybrids and other cultivars of ''V. darrowii'' (southern highbush blueberry) have been developed for cultivation in warm southern and western regions of North America.<ref>[http://www.extension.org/pages/.../southern-highbush-blueberry-varieties eXtension: Southern Highbush Blueberry Varieties]{{Dead link|date=January 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}}</ref><ref>[http://www.fourwindsgrowers.com/pdfs/blueberry_information.pdf Four Winds Growers: Care of southern highbush blueberries]</ref>

== Uses ==
The edible berries<ref name="kemper" /> were collected and used in [[Native American cuisine]] in areas where ''V. corymbosum'' grew natively.<ref>[http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Vaccinium+corymbosum University of Michigan at Dearborn — Native American Ethnobotany of ''Vaccinium corymbosum''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130529014226/http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Vaccinium+corymbosum |date=2013-05-29}}. accessed 9.9.2015</ref>
